Q114.L1t: Semiconductors are materials whose conductivity lies between that of metals and insulators and can be tuned by adding impurity atoms.
Q114.L2t: Doping adds donor or acceptor atoms that supply extra electrons or holes, which changes the carrier concentration and the conductivity of the material.
Q114.L3t: When current flows through a conductor in a transverse magnetic field, the Lorentz force pushes the moving carriers sideways, building a transverse voltage whose polarity depends on whether the carriers are positive or negative.
Q114.L4t: The sign of the carriers is found by measuring the transverse voltage-based coefficient that appears when current flows in a magnetic field, namely the Hall coefficient.
Q114.L2f: In a doped semiconductor, the carrier concentration is fixed by temperature alone and is unaffected by the density of donor or acceptor impurities.
Q114.L3f: The response of a material to an applied magnetic field, whether it is attracted or repelled, switches sign directly with the sign of the mobile charge carriers, so it reveals their sign.
Q114.L4f: The sign of the carriers is revealed by measuring how the material responds to an applied magnetic field in terms of its magnetic susceptibility.

Q115.L1t: Special relativity predicts that lengths measured along the direction of relative motion differ from lengths measured in the object's rest frame.
Q115.L2t: Length contraction applies only to the dimension parallel to the relative velocity, and the rest length is the longest length any observer can measure.
Q115.L3t: The contracted length equals the rest length times the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, so a ratio of 0.80 requires the square root term to equal 0.80, which means v²/c² = 0.36.
Q115.L4t: The observer must move at six-tenths of the speed of light.
Q115.L2f: Length contraction in special relativity affects dimensions perpendicular to the motion as well as the parallel one, and the rest length is the shortest length any observer can measure.
Q115.L3f: The contracted length equals the rest length times the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, and a ratio of 0.80 is obtained when v²/c² = 0.75, so the speed is lower than most would expect.
Q115.L4f: The observer must move at half the speed of light, which is the speed that shortens the rod to 0.80 m.

Q116.L1t: The cosmic microwave background is thermal radiation left over from the early universe, and it has cooled as the universe has expanded.
Q116.L2t: The CMB has a blackbody spectrum, and its temperature today is measured to be about 2.7 K.
Q116.L3t: The temperature of the background radiation is inversely proportional to the scale factor of the universe, so a fourfold higher temperature (12 K versus 3 K) corresponds to a scale factor four times smaller.
Q116.L4t: At 12 K, typical separations between galaxies were one-quarter of what they are today.
Q116.L2f: The CMB was emitted by hot stars in the first galaxies, and its spectrum is not a blackbody, so it has no simple relation to the universe's expansion.
Q116.L3f: The radiation temperature is directly proportional to the scale factor of the universe, so a fourfold higher temperature means the universe was four times larger, and distances between galaxies were correspondingly greater.
Q116.L4f: At 12 K, typical galaxies were separated by twice the distances we see today, since the universe has contracted as it cooled.
